rows.reference: Exodus 20:13 (Hebrew and English numbering agree; parallel Deuteronomy 5:17, not checked). The Septuagint is reported to put the commandments in a different order, so the verse number in Brenton may differ (not checked)
rows.original: לֹא תִּרְצָח (lo tirtsach)
rows.translation: KJV "Thou shalt not kill" and NASB "You shall not murder", as displayed on Bible Hub; WEBBE wording not displayed
rows.says: You shall not murder. Most modern versions render the verb as "murder" (unlawful killing); the KJV and Douay-Rheims keep "kill".
rows.bearing: Teaches K1 and K0 (rule 7), Explicit, for all branches. The verse does not itself say who is protected; Genesis 9:5 to 6 (next row) gives it universal reach. The tradition reads "murder" as unjust killing and names courts, war and defence as the cases outside it (Augustine, City of God I.21; Westminster Larger Catechism Q.136), which is K1's own structure with exclusions (a) and (b). Whether any other private killing falls outside "murder" is the question the counter rows test.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): Bible Hub's comparison page showed the Hebrew לֹא תִּרְצָח with KJV "Thou shalt not kill" and NASB "You shall not murder"; Bible Gateway's verse page also returned

rows.original: כִּי בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם (for in the image of God He made humankind)
rows.translation: KJV, as displayed on Biblia and Bible Study Tools; ESV compared
rows.says: God will demand an account for every human life, "at the hand of every man's brother". Whoever sheds human blood, by a human his blood shall be shed, because God made people in His own image.
rows.bearing: Teaches K1 (rule 7), Explicit. It is spoken to Noah, so to all humanity, and grounds the protection in the image of God that every person bears. So it reaches every person K1 protects, whatever their faith, status, sex or age. The penalty clause ("by man shall his blood be shed") is read by the tradition as a mandate for public justice. That part is context only (exclusion (a), rule 5).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): KJV wording of 9:5 to 6, including "at the hand of every man's brother" and "in the image of God made he man", confirmed on Biblia and Bible Study Tools

rows.original: Οὐ φονεύσεις ... πᾶς ὁ ὀργιζόμενος τῷ ἀδελφῷ αὐτοῦ
rows.translation: KJV (1900 text, Biblia); NASB and ESV compared
rows.says: Jesus repeats "You shall not murder" and goes further: anyone who is angry with his brother is liable to judgement, and contemptuous insults are judged more severely. The KJV's "without a cause" is a reading many older manuscripts lack.
rows.bearing: Teaches K0 (killing out of anger) and K1 (rule 7), Explicit. It is a wider duty: it forbids even the anger that leads to killing. On its own "brother" might be read narrowly, but the same sermon extends love to enemies (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:27 to 35, row below), so it reaches everyone.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): Biblia (KJV 1900, NASB 1995, ESV, NIV) for 5:21 to 22, including the "without a cause" variant

rows.says: Asked what to do to have eternal life, Jesus lists the commandments, beginning "You shall not murder".

rows.original: ἡ ἀγάπη τῷ πλησίον κακὸν οὐκ ἐργάζεται (love does no harm to a neighbour)
rows.says: "Thou shalt not kill" and the other commandments are summed up in "love your neighbour as yourself"; love does no harm to a neighbour.
rows.bearing: Teaches K1 and K0 (rule 7), Explicit, as a wider duty not to harm (METHOD.md section 3). In Christian reading "neighbour" reaches everyone (Luke 10:29 to 37; see sources/translations.md), so it is not limited to some people.

rows.original: ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν (love your enemies)
rows.translation: World English Bible; KJV (as in Article I)
rows.says: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and treat others as you want to be treated.
rows.bearing: A wider duty that reaches enemies, the people most likely to be killed out of hatred or revenge. So it teaches K0 and supports K1's reach (rule 7, Clear teaching). It also asks more than K1, which the floor allows.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search), partial: Article I row 9a (Bible Gateway link to Luke 6:31; the surrounding commands to love enemies are summarised there). Matthew 5:44 not checked

rows.original: קוֹל דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ צֹעֲקִים אֵלַי מִן הָאֲדָמָה (the voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground)
rows.translation: KJV (sacred-texts.com; King James Bible Online); ESV compared
rows.says: Cain is "very wroth" when his offering is not accepted, and kills his brother Abel. God says Abel's blood cries out from the ground and curses Cain.
rows.bearing: Teaches K0 (killing out of anger and envy) and K1 (rule 7). The story condemns the first killing in scripture, and God himself judges it wrong. 1 John 3:12 uses it as the model of murder.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): KJV of Genesis 4:5 to 11, with "Cain was very wroth" (4:5) and the blood crying from the ground (4:10), on sacred-texts.com and King James Bible Online

rows.original: πᾶς ὁ μισῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ ἀνθρωποκτόνος ἐστίν
rows.translation: ASV and ESV, as displayed (ASV wording matches the KJV)
rows.says: Do not be like Cain, who murdered his brother. Anyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and no murderer has eternal life in him.
rows.bearing: Teaches K0 (killing out of hatred) and K1 (rule 7), Explicit: hatred is named as murder at its root. Limit: in this letter "brother" may mean a fellow believer, so on its own this text could be "taught in part". Its reach to everyone rests on Genesis 9:6 and the commands to love enemies.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): ESV.org showed 3:12 and 3:15; the ASV wording of 3:15 was confirmed in the results

rows.original: וַתְּחַיֶּיןָ אֶת הַיְלָדִים (they kept the boys alive)
rows.says: Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives to kill newborn boys at birth. They fear God, disobey, and save the children alive, and God deals well with them.
rows.bearing: Teaches K1 for newborns (rules 7 and 9), Clear teaching: God rewards refusing to kill infants at birth. The order came from a ruler, but the text approves refusing it, so it supports K1 and does not fall under exclusion (a).

rows.says: Sacrificing one's own sons and daughters is condemned as shedding innocent blood.
rows.bearing: Would teach K1 for children from birth (rules 7 and 9), Explicit, against killing by parents. It is UNVERIFIED, so it does not count (rule 1).

rows.says: If a master strikes his male or female slave with a rod and the slave dies under his hand, the master shall surely be punished.
rows.bearing: Teaches K1 for slaves (rule 7), Explicit: killing one's own slave is a crime. Verse 21 limits this (see the limit row below).

rows.original: אֵת אוּרִיָּה הַחִתִּי הִכִּיתָ בַחֶרֶב (Uriah the Hittite you struck with the sword)
rows.translation: KJV; World English Bible ("struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword"), as displayed on Bible Gateway and Bible Hub
rows.says: The prophet Nathan, sent by God, condemns King David for having Uriah the Hittite killed by the sword of the Ammonites so that he could take Uriah's wife.
rows.bearing: Teaches K0 (killing for gain) and K1 (rule 7), Clear teaching. The victim is a foreigner, so the protection reaches strangers. Arranging a death through a staged battle is still condemned, so a ruler cannot hide a private motive behind war or office.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): KJV and WEB of 12:9 on Bible Gateway and Bible Hub

rows.original: וְדָם נָקִי אַל תִּשְׁפְּכוּ בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה (and do not shed innocent blood in this place)
rows.translation: KJV (King James Bible Online; Bible Gateway); ESV, NIV, NASB compared
rows.says: The king and his house are told to do justice, rescue the robbed, do no wrong or violence to the stranger, the fatherless or the widow, and not to shed innocent blood.
rows.bearing: Teaches K1 (rule 7), Explicit. The stranger is named among the protected, and the command binds rulers as well as private people.

rows.translation: KJV (Bible Study Tools); ESV and NLT compared
rows.says: Cursed is anyone who takes payment to kill an innocent person, and all the people answer "Amen".

rows.original: μὴ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκδικοῦντες, ἀγαπητοί (do not avenge yourselves, beloved)
rows.translation: KJV (Bible Study Tools; kjvstudy); ESV compared
rows.says: Do not take revenge yourselves; leave room for God's wrath, for "Vengeance is mine" (Deuteronomy 32:35). Do not repay evil for evil, and feed your enemy (12:17 and 12:20, not checked).

rows.translation: JPS 1917 (Sefaria), as in Article I row 2b
rows.says: Do not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the children of your people; love your neighbour as yourself.
rows.bearing: Teaches the revenge part of K0 (rule 7), Explicit. On its own words it names fellow Israelites, so alone it is taught in part. Christian reading widens "neighbour" to everyone (Luke 10:29 to 37), and Romans 12:19 states the rule with no limit.

rows.reference: Luke 9:51 to 56 (the longer saying in 9:55b to 56a is a textual variant)
rows.original: στραφεὶς δὲ ἐπετίμησεν αὐτοῖς (he turned and rebuked them)
rows.translation: ESV with footnote (Biblia); KJV (Bible Study Tools) for the longer reading
rows.says: A Samaritan village refuses to receive Jesus. James and John ask whether to call down fire from heaven to destroy it, and Jesus turns and rebukes them. Some manuscripts add: "the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them".
rows.bearing: Teaches K1 and K0 (rule 7), Clear teaching. People of another religious community who reject the founder are not to be destroyed out of anger, so the protection reaches outsiders and "heretics" (Samaritans were seen as such). Only the rebuke counts. The explicit saying is missing from many of the oldest Greek manuscripts and should not be relied on.

rows.translation: Roberts and Donaldson (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7), as reproduced; Lightfoot (1891) not displayed
rows.says: Among the commands of the "way of life": do not murder, and do not murder a child by abortion or kill one that has been born.

rows.tier: 2 (not counted; Church Father honoured by all branches, especially in the West)
rows.reference: Augustine, City of God I.21 (with I.20)
rows.original: Non occides ("Thou shalt not kill", as Augustine quotes it)
rows.translation: Marcus Dods (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 2), on Wikisource and Logos Virtual Library
rows.says: The command not to kill has exceptions only by divine authority: a just general law (soldiers and officials acting for public justice, who are like a sword in another's hand), or a special command God gives for a time to a person (Abraham's readiness to sacrifice Isaac; Samson). Anyone else who kills a person, himself or another, is guilty of murder.
rows.bearing: The tradition's classical reading. It applies Exodus 20:13 to every private killing and allows only public justice and war (exclusions (a) and (b)) and special divine commands, which bear on the hard cases (Genesis 22; the war commands). It names no private right to kill in self-defence. Not counted (rule 1). Killing oneself (I.20) is context only (exclusion (d)).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): chapter title and contents (the two kinds of exception, the officer as sword, Abraham, Jephthah and Samson, and the closing rule) shown from Wikisource's NPNF text and Logos Virtual Library

rows.tier: 2 (not counted; Catholic branch only)
rows.reference: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II q.64 a.3, a.6, a.7
rows.original: Utrum liceat alicui occidere hominem se defendendo (a.7 title, from memory)
rows.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent; CCEL
rows.says: Question 64 ("Of murder") asks whether killing a sinner is lawful for a private individual or only for a public person (a.3), whether it is lawful to kill a just man (a.6), and whether it is lawful to kill in self-defence (a.7). Article 7's objections cite Augustine (to Publicola) as allowing this only to soldiers and public officials. From memory, NOT displayed: the answers are that only public authority may kill an evildoer, that killing the innocent is never lawful, and that self-defence is lawful with proportionate force when the attacker's death is not intended.
rows.bearing: For Catholics, this states K1's exact structure: no private killing, the innocent never, a defence exception, and courts kept to public authority. It is branch-only and not counted (rules 1 and 3), and its answers are unverified.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) for the question's structure and the article titles (New Advent q.64 index; CCEL a.7 with its objection citing Augustine to Publicola). UNVERIFIED: the text of the answers in a.3, a.6 and a.7

It does not contradict K1. Catholic, Orthodox and mainstream Protestant authorities read it as personal restraint, not as abolishing public force (Augustine, City of God I.21). Peace churches read it as forbidding all killing. It is UNVERIFIED.

rows.bearing: Limits equal protection for slaves. For K1 it bears as Unclear at most (rule 6), not Contradicted. The text concerns a beating, and the contrast with an immediate death (21:20) is widely read as a question of intent, so whether it reaches a deliberate killing is disputed, and an unintended death falls under exclusion (f). Article I's annex counted it as contradicting a no-cruelty wording, which is a different question.

rows.original: אֵין לוֹ דָּם (there is no blood for him, that is, no bloodguilt)
rows.translation: KJV (Christianity.com; Bible Hub); English Revised and Webster compared
rows.says: If someone who killed by accident leaves his city of refuge and the next of kin, the "avenger of blood" (go'el ha-dam), finds and kills him there, the avenger "shall not be guilty of blood". Verses 19 and 21 say the avenger himself shall kill a murderer when he meets him.
rows.bearing: This is the strongest counted text against K1 and K0 found in this search. A kinsman, whom rule 5 names as a private actor, is declared blameless for killing a person who killed by accident and is no threat. Under rules 2 and 5 that points to Contradicted, for all branches. Against that reading, the same chapter has the congregation judge between slayer and avenger (35:24 to 25) and requires witnesses (35:30), so the avenger can be read as the law's appointed executor (exclusion (a)). If it is disputed whether the killing is judicial or private, the label is Unclear (rule 5). Christian authorities hold that Israel's judicial laws no longer bind (Aquinas I-II q.104 a.3), but under Article I's annex precedent and decision 7 that does not remove a contradiction. No Christian commentary on the avenger was searched.

support.reconciliation:
Christianity reconciles its hard texts on killing in four ways. Each source and its standing are given below; none of these authorities is a counted text.
(1) The commandment is read as a total ban on private killing, with only two kinds of exception, both resting on divine authority. These are public justice and just war (a just general law), and a special command God gives to a particular person for a time (Abraham, Samson, and by extension the war commands and similar acts). Source: Augustine, City of God I.21 (Tier 2, a Father honoured by all branches; verified by search on Wikisource). Augustine's list gives no private right to kill in self-defence, and his Letter 47 to Publicola doubts that one exists (known here only as cited in Aquinas II-II q.64 a.7, objection; verified as cited).
(2) The Old Testament's judicial laws are held to bind no longer. These include the avenger of blood (Numbers 35), the stoning of an enticer (Deuteronomy 13) and the household laws of Exodus 21. Sources: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II q.104 a.3 (Catholic; verified by search in Article I's annex) and the Westminster Confession 19.4 (Reformed; unverified). Under Article I's annex precedent and METHOD.md decision 7, this ends their binding force without saying that what they permitted was wrong, so it does not remove a contradiction in a counted text.
(3) The New Testament, counted by every branch, gives punishment to public authority and forbids private revenge. See Romans 12:19 (verified), Romans 13:4 (unverified) and the commands to love enemies (Luke 6:27 to 35, verified in Article I).
(4) Each branch states K1's structure in its own authorities. For Catholics, Aquinas II-II q.64: no private person may kill even an evildoer (a.3); the innocent may never be killed (a.6); self-defence is allowed with proportionate force, without intending death (a.7). The article titles were verified by search but the answers were not. For Reformed Protestants, the Westminster Larger Catechism Q.136: all taking of life is forbidden \"except in case of public justice, lawful war, or necessary defence\" (seen only on non-reference transcriptions). No Orthodox authority (for example the canons of Basil on homicide, or the Fathers on soldiers) was checked.
On war, the tradition treats the commands to destroy whole peoples (1 Samuel 15:3; Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17; Numbers 31:17) as special divine commissions for that time, not a rule for others (Augustine, City of God I.21). Just-war teaching (Augustine; Aquinas II-II q.40, not checked) and, for Catholics, the Catechism (2313 to 2314, unverified) protect non-combatants. These later authorities do not outweigh the counted texts for K3 (decision 7).

K1.label: Unclear (provisional; Taught on the support evidence alone)
K1.reason: Counted Tier 1 texts accepted by every branch teach K1 explicitly (rule 7). Exodus 20:13 forbids murder, and Genesis 9:5 to 6 extends the protection to every human being, as made in God's image. The New Testament repeats it and widens it to a duty of no harm and love of enemies (Matthew 5:21 to 22; Romans 13:8 to 10; Luke 6:27 to 35). Named groups are protected: newborns (Exodus 1:15 to 21, rule 9), slaves (Exodus 21:20), foreigners (2 Samuel 12:9; Jeremiah 22:3) and religious outsiders (Luke 9:51 to 56). The tradition's authorities state K1's exact structure (Augustine, City of God I.21; Aquinas II-II q.64; Westminster Larger Catechism Q.136). However, Numbers 35:26 to 27 (verified, Tier 1, all branches) says a kinsman who kills an accidental slayer outside a city of refuge "shall not be guilty of blood". If the avenger is a private person, that is Contradicted under rules 2 and 5. If he is the law's executor, it is context under exclusion (a). Numbers 25 and Deuteronomy 13 (unverified) raise the same judicial or private question. Under rule 5's last sentence that makes the label Unclear. Aquinas's annulment of the judicial laws does not change this (decision 7; Article I's annex precedent). If the counter researcher finds Christian authority treating the avenger's killing as a lawful private act, the label should be Contradicted (all branches). If the avenger is read as the court's executor, the label should be Taught. Exodus 21:21 is at most Unclear (intent disputed; exclusion (f)), and Genesis 22 is Implied (rule 4).

K0.label: Unclear (provisional; Taught on the support evidence alone)
K0.reason: K0 is taught explicitly in counted texts of every branch for each of its motives. Anger: Matthew 5:21 to 22 and Genesis 4. Hatred: 1 John 3:15 (whose "brother" may mean fellow believers) with Luke 6:27 to 35 on enemies. Gain: Deuteronomy 27:25 and 2 Samuel 12:9. Revenge: Romans 12:19 and Leviticus 19:18. The same hard case applies as for K1, and more sharply, because the go'el is literally the blood avenger. Numbers 35:19 and 21 let him kill a murderer, which may be judicial (Deuteronomy 19:12, unverified, has the elders hand the murderer over). Numbers 35:27 declares him guiltless for killing an accidental slayer outside the refuge. Whether that is a private revenge killing or a legal execution is unresolved (rules 5 and 6). Deuteronomy 19:6 (unverified) says the slayer did not deserve death, which, if verified, supports a narrowing reading.

K3.label: Contradicted (all branches), provisional
K3.reason: In Numbers 31:17, a counted Tier 1 text accepted by every branch, the lawgiver orders the killing of captured boys and of women. It is VERIFIED (search) only through Article I's annex row JU-17, whose link is to 31:18, and rule 4 is met. 1 Samuel 15:3 (infants and nursing babies) and Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17 (nothing that breathes) are divine commands to the same effect, but are unverified here. Partial support exists in Tier 1 (Deuteronomy 20:10 to 14; 2 Kings 6:21 to 23, both unverified). For Catholics the Catechism (2313 to 2314, unverified) teaches K3. The tradition reads the war commands as one-time divine commissions (Augustine, City of God I.21, verified), but later authorities do not outweigh a counted text (decision 7). K3 is a record wording and does not affect the floor.

rows.reference: Numbers 25:1 to 13, especially 25:4 to 8 and 25:10 to 13 (same numbering in the Hebrew, the Septuagint and the Vulgate)
rows.original: בְּקַנְאוֹ אֶת קִנְאָתִי (be-qanno et qin'ati, 'in being zealous with my zeal', 25:11)
rows.translation: World English Bible (British Edition), paraphrased; content as shown in commentary pages on Numbers 25
rows.says: Israelite men join in the worship of Baal Peor and a plague breaks out. God tells Moses to hang the chiefs, and Moses tells Israel's judges to kill each man who joined Baal Peor (25:4 to 5). An Israelite man then brings a Midianite woman into his tent in sight of everyone. Phinehas, grandson of Aaron the priest, follows with a spear and kills them both, and the plague stops. God says Phinehas turned his anger away by being zealous with God's zeal, and gives him a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood.
rows.bearing: K1: the hardest text. God approves, in words, the deliberate killing of two people who were not attacking anyone, done without a trial. If Phinehas acted as a private zealot, this would contradict K1 in every branch (rule 2). But the tradition disputes whether the act was private. It comes straight after Moses' order to the judges (25:5). Phinehas was of the priestly line. Psalm 106:30 is rendered 'executed judgment' in some versions (row 2). One commentary in the search results reads the repeated genealogy as a sign of public authority, while Matthew Henry treats the act as extraordinary zeal that 'can never be an example' for private revenge (row 35). So rule 5 (last sentence) and rule 6 apply, and the label is Unclear. The victims are an Israelite man and a foreign woman, so protection is not limited to one's own community. K0: the motive given is zeal for God, not gain, anger, hatred or revenge in the personal sense; it bears on K0 only if zeal is read as anger (Implied). K3: not war in this passage (the war on Midian follows at 25:16 to 18 and in chapter 31).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search), partial: commentary pages on Numbers 25 in the search results confirmed that Phinehas took a spear (javelin), killed Zimri and Cozbi out of zeal and was rewarded with a covenant of priesthood. Those pages were John Gill on sacred-texts.com, Matthew Henry's note on openbible.com and christianity.com, and Calvin's Harmony on sacred-texts.com. The verse page itself was not seen. Verses 25:4 to 5, 'covenant of peace' and the Hebrew phrase are from memory and were not checked.

rows.reference: Psalm 106:28 to 31 (Septuagint and Vulgate Psalm 105:28 to 31; Douay-Rheims Psalm 105)
rows.original: וַיַּעֲמֹד פִּינְחָס וַיְפַלֵּל (va-ya'amod Pinchas va-yefallel); Septuagint καὶ ἔστη Φινεες καὶ ἐξιλάσατο
rows.says: Looking back on Baal Peor, the psalm says Phinehas stood up and 'executed judgment' (KJV), the plague stopped, and this was counted to him as righteousness for all generations. Other versions render the verb 'intervened' or 'interposed'; the Septuagint has 'made atonement' and the Vulgate (Douay-Rheims) 'pacified'.
rows.bearing: K1: repeats God's approval of Phinehas (row 1) in a second book of shared scripture, with the formula 'counted to him for righteousness'. The verb (pillel) is disputed. 'Executed judgment' presents the act as judicial; 'intervened', 'made atonement' and 'pacified' do not. A disputed word that bears on whether the killing was judicial or private makes the label Unclear (rules 5 and 6), not Contradicted. Note that verse 38 of the same psalm condemns child sacrifice as shedding innocent blood (row 28). K0, K3: no bearing.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched, because the shared web search limit was reached. The renderings of pillel and the Septuagint and Vulgate readings are from memory.

rows.tier: 1 (Catholic and Orthodox only; Apocrypha for Protestants)
rows.reference: 1 Maccabees 2:15 to 28 and 2:49 to 54; Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 45:23 to 24 (verse numbers differ between Greek-based and Vulgate-based editions)
rows.translation: KJV Apocrypha and Douay-Rheims, paraphrased from memory
rows.says: A king's officer orders the people of Modein to sacrifice to idols. A Jew steps forward to sacrifice, and Mattathias, burning with zeal, kills him on the altar and kills the officer, acting for the law 'as Phinehas did' to Zimri. He then calls everyone zealous for the law to follow him, which begins the Maccabean revolt. On his deathbed Mattathias names Phinehas as a model of zeal. Sirach praises Phinehas for his zeal and for making atonement for Israel.
rows.bearing: K1: the narrative approves, by comparing it with Phinehas, a private killing of a fellow Jew who was sacrificing and not attacking anyone. But it is also the first act of a war of resistance against a ruler who was enforcing idolatry, and the officer was that ruler's agent. Whether it is a private killing or an act of war is therefore disputed: Unclear for the Catholic and Orthodox branches (rules 3, 5 and 6). Under the corpus rule, no finding for Christianity may rest on these texts alone, and Protestants do not count them. K3: war context. K0: zeal, not gain or revenge.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (approval by comparison), if verified
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched; content and verse numbers are from memory.

rows.reference: 1 Kings 18:36 to 40, with 18:41, 19:1 and 19:10 to 18 (Septuagint 3 Kingdoms; Douay-Rheims 3 Kings)
rows.original: וַיִּשְׁחָטֵם שָׁם (va-yishchatem sham, 'and he slaughtered them there', 18:40)
rows.says: After fire from heaven answers Elijah on Mount Carmel, Elijah tells the people to seize the prophets of Baal and let none escape. He takes them down to the brook Kishon and kills them there. King Ahab is present at Carmel (18:41). Before the fire, Elijah prays that it be known he has done 'all these things' at God's word (18:36). Later Elijah tells God he has been very zealous, and God sends him to anoint new kings and a prophet.
rows.bearing: K1: a religious leader has a crowd seize religious opponents, who were not attacking anyone, and kills them. No verse says God commanded or approved the killing itself; 18:36 refers to the contest, before it. So under rule 4 the passage is a report: Implied, and it does not decide. If it were read as approved, it would be disputed whether this was a private act or an application of the law against false prophets (Deuteronomy 13:1 to 5; 18:20) with the king present (rule 5), which would make it Unclear. The tradition's own counter-reading is Jesus' rebuke of disciples who wanted to copy Elijah (row 5). Protection by faith: the victims die for their religion. K0: no gain, anger or revenge in the text.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched; content from memory.

rows.original: στραφεὶς δὲ ἐπετίμησεν αὐτοῖς (he turned and rebuked them, 9:55)
rows.says: A Samaritan village refuses to receive Jesus. James and John ask whether they should call down fire from heaven to destroy it; many manuscripts add 'as Elijah did'. Jesus turns and rebukes them, and they go to another village. The longer KJV wording ('Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them') is a variant missing from critical editions.
rows.bearing: Reconciliation. It is Clear teaching, in texts every branch accepts, that disciples must not destroy religious outsiders out of their own zeal, and it rejects Elijah's example used that way. Elijah's fire is 2 Kings 1:10 to 12, not the killing at Kishon, so linking it to row 4 is the tradition's reading, not the text's. It supports K1 (outsiders and unbelievers are protected; religious zeal is no licence) and K0. Matthew Henry (Protestant) reads it as condemning furious zeal.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in earlier project research (Article I, 13 October 2026), not re-checked in this run: Bible Gateway, Luke 9:55, with the variant noted; Matthew Henry on Luke 9:51 to 56 on Bible Gateway.

rows.reference: Numbers 35:9 to 34, especially 35:12, 15, 19, 21 and 24 to 27; Deuteronomy 19:1 to 13, especially 19:6 and 19:11 to 13
rows.original: גֹּאֵל הַדָּם הוּא יָמִית אֶת הָרֹצֵחַ (go'el ha-dam hu yamit et ha-rotseach, 'the avenger of blood himself shall put the murderer to death', 35:19); אֵין לוֹ דָּם (ein lo dam, 'he has no blood-guilt', 35:27)
rows.translation: KJV ('revenger of blood'); World English Bible ('avenger of blood')
rows.says: The 'avenger of blood', the dead person's next of kin, is to put a murderer to death himself when he meets him (35:19, 21). Someone who killed without intent may flee to a city of refuge. The congregation judges between him and the avenger (35:12, 24 to 25), and he must stay in the city until the high priest dies. If he leaves it and the avenger kills him, the avenger is not guilty of blood (35:27). Deuteronomy warns that the avenger may pursue the slayer 'while his heart is hot' (19:6), and has the elders hand a deliberate murderer over to the avenger (19:11 to 13). Strangers and sojourners may use the cities of refuge too (35:15).
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a kinsman may kill a person who is not attacking anyone, on a footing the law itself calls avenging. Verse 35:27 declares blameless the killing of someone who killed by accident, because of where he was found. Yet the law sets all this inside a procedure (the congregation's judgement, the cities of refuge, the elders), so whether the avenger acts as a private person or as the law's executor is disputed: Unclear (rules 5 and 6), not Contradicted. The New Testament narrows it: vengeance belongs to God and to the ruler, who is 'a revenger to execute wrath' (Romans 12:19 to 13:4, row 22). The main Catholic and Reformed authorities hold that these judicial laws no longer bind (row 34). Protection is not limited to one's own community (35:15). Because it is unverified, this row does not decide a label yet (rule 1).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched in this run, because the shared web search limit was reached. An earlier project check (Article I) also left Numbers 35:19 to 21 unverified.

rows.reference: Deuteronomy 13:6 to 11 (Hebrew 13:7 to 12), with 13:1 to 5, 17:2 to 7 and Exodus 22:18 and 22:20 (Hebrew 22:17 and 22:19)
rows.original: כִּי הָרֹג תַּהַרְגֶנּוּ (ki harog taharegennu, 'you shall surely kill him', Hebrew 13:10); Septuagint ἀναγγέλλων ἀναγγελεῖς περὶ αὐτοῦ ('you shall surely report concerning him')
rows.translation: KJV and World English Bible (Hebrew text); L. C. L. Brenton (Septuagint)
rows.says: If a brother, son, daughter, wife or closest friend secretly urges you to serve other gods, you must not pity or shield them. The Hebrew text says 'you shall surely kill him; your hand shall be first upon him', then the hand of all the people, and he is stoned. The Septuagint, which the Orthodox branch treats as authoritative, reads 'you shall surely report concerning him' before the same stoning. Deuteronomy 17:2 to 7 requires two or three witnesses and a judgement at the city gates before anyone is stoned for serving other gods. Exodus 22 sets death for sorcery and for sacrificing to other gods.
rows.bearing: K1: a family member is to be killed for religious enticement, with no attack. On the Hebrew wording it can read as a private killing by the relative. The Septuagint's 'report' and Deuteronomy 17:2 to 7 place it in a judicial process. Because it is disputed whether this is judicial or private, the label would be Unclear (rules 5 and 6); if read with 17:2 to 7, it is court context (exclusion (a)). It also grades protection by faith (the apostate or enticer). K0: no gain, anger or revenge. Christian reconciliation: the judicial laws no longer bind (row 34), and Luke 9:54 to 55 applies (row 5). Because it is unverified, this row does not decide a label yet (rule 1).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched in this run. The Hebrew and Septuagint readings are from memory and must be checked in Brenton before use.

rows.original: וְהִרְגוּ אִישׁ אֶת אָחִיו (and kill every man his brother, 32:27)
rows.says: After the golden calf, Moses stands at the camp gate, says 'Thus says the LORD', and tells the Levites to go through the camp and kill brother, friend and neighbour. About three thousand die. Moses tells them they have consecrated themselves to the LORD that day.
rows.bearing: Context (rule 5): the order comes from Moses as leader of the people, in God's name, so it falls under exclusion (a) as a ruler's order. If Moses is read as a religious leader rather than a ruler, it becomes a hard case for K1 (Unclear, rule 6). Aquinas raises this text as the first objection to his rule that only public authority may kill (row 30). His reply (that those who kill at God's command act by God's authority, following Augustine) was not seen in search. K0, K3: no direct bearing.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search), indirectly: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II q.64 a.3, objection 1, cites Exodus 32:27 as Moses' command to kill one's neighbours over the golden calf (ccel.org). The verse page itself was not seen; 32:29 is from memory.

rows.original: נָקֹם יִנָּקֵם (naqom yinnaqem, 'he shall surely be avenged', 21:20); כִּי כַסְפּוֹ הוּא ('for he is his money', 21:21)
rows.translation: NKJV and KJV (as checked in Article I's households annex)
rows.says: A master who strikes his slave with a rod so that the slave dies under his hand must be punished. If the slave survives a day or two, the master is not punished, 'for he is his money'. By contrast, 21:12 sets death for anyone who strikes a man so that he dies.
rows.bearing: Graded protection (rule 2), not permission. Killing a slave outright is punished, but the protection is weaker than for a free person. Death after a day or two is treated as unintended (exclusion (f)), not as a licence to kill. Does not contradict K1 or K0; it limits equal protection by status. The main authorities hold that this law no longer binds (row 34).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in Article I's households annex (row CH-1), not re-checked in this run: Biblia, NKJV.

rows.original: אֵין לוֹ דָּמִים (ein lo damim, 'there is no blood-guilt for him')
rows.says: If a thief is caught breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there is no blood-guilt. But if the sun has risen on him, there is blood-guilt.
rows.bearing: K1: declares a killing blameless because of what the victim was doing. Jewish and Christian commentators commonly read the line between day and night as marking a burglar who may threaten life, when the householder cannot see or get help. On that reading the text sits inside K1's exception for defence, and even narrows it, since by day the killer is guilty. That reading was not verified in a Christian source here. At most a hard case (rule 6), not a contradiction. K0: protecting the daytime thief shows that killing only to protect property is not blameless.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched; the commentary reading is from memory.

rows.reference: Genesis 22:1 to 19, with Hebrews 11:17 to 19 and James 2:21
rows.says: God tells Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a burnt offering. Abraham binds him and takes the knife, but an angel stops him and a ram is offered instead. The New Testament praises Abraham's faith in being ready to offer his son.
rows.bearing: K1 (children): the text approves a father's readiness to kill his child at God's command, but no killing takes place, and God himself stops it at the end. Under rule 4 it is Implied for any contradiction and does not decide. It is the classic hard case for a divine-command exception, which Aquinas uses: Abraham did not sin in consenting, because God is Lord of life and death (row 31). The same scriptures condemn child sacrifice outright elsewhere (row 28).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED for the verses (not searched). Aquinas's use of the episode was confirmed (row 31).

rows.says: Jephthah vows to offer to God whatever first comes out of his house if he wins. His daughter comes out, and after two months he 'did with her according to his vow'. The text reports this without praise or blame. Hebrews later lists Jephthah among people of faith, for his deeds in war.
rows.bearing: K1 (children): a father kills his daughter to keep a vow (on a minority reading, he dedicates her to lifelong virginity instead). The text reports the act and does not approve it: Implied (rule 4), does not decide. Christian reconciliation (UNVERIFIED): Jerome, quoted by Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II q.88 a.2 ad 2), says Jephthah was foolish in making the vow and wicked in keeping it; Augustine (City of God I.21) leaves open whether he acted at God's command.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.reference: Judges 14:4 and 14:19; 15:7 to 8, 15:11 and 15:20; 16:28 to 30; with Hebrews 11:32 to 34
rows.original: וַתִּצְלַח עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה (the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, 14:19)
rows.says: The text says God was seeking an occasion against the Philistines, who ruled Israel (14:4). The Spirit of the LORD comes on Samson, and he kills thirty men of Ashkelon and gives their garments to those who solved his riddle (14:19). He later kills Philistines, saying 'as they did to me, so I have done to them' (15:11). At the end he prays to be avenged for his eyes and pulls the temple down on himself and them (16:28 to 30). He judged Israel for twenty years, and Hebrews lists him among people of faith.
rows.bearing: K0: the motives named include paying a debt (gain) and revenge, and the first killing follows the Spirit's coming. The tradition reads Samson as a judge and deliverer in Israel's war against Philistine rule, acting by divine prompting (Augustine, City of God I.21, on his death; UNVERIFIED). So this is war context (exclusion (b)) or a disputed hard case: Unclear at most (rules 5 and 6), not Contradicted. K3: the thirty men of Ashkelon were not fighting, but the text does not say in words that the act was right: Implied against K3. K1: as K0. His own death falls under exclusion (d).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.says: Moses sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, looks around, kills the Egyptian and hides him in the sand. When it becomes known, he flees. In Acts, Stephen says Moses defended the man who was wronged and avenged him, supposing his people would understand that God was delivering them by his hand.
rows.bearing: K1: a private killing. The beating may make it defence of another (inside K1's exception), or it may be vengeance. Acts reports Moses' purpose without plainly approving the act: Implied (rule 4), does not decide. Reconciliation (UNVERIFIED): Augustine (Contra Faustum XXII.70) judges the act a fault, done without lawful authority, though it showed a spirit fit to be trained. Calvin's Harmony of the Law also discusses Moses' zeal here; this was seen in a search result only as a topic, without its content.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched. The search for Augustine was refused because the shared web search limit was reached.

rows.reference: Deuteronomy 21:18 to 21; Exodus 21:15 and 21:17; Leviticus 20:9; Matthew 15:3 to 6 and Mark 7:9 to 13
rows.says: Parents of a stubborn, rebellious son who will not obey are to bring him to the elders at the city gate, and the men of the city stone him. Whoever strikes or curses father or mother is to be put to death. Jesus quotes 'he who curses father or mother, let him die' while rebuking people who use a religious gift to avoid supporting their parents.
rows.bearing: Context only (rule 5). The parents start the case, but the elders and the community decide and carry it out, so this is a court procedure (exclusion (a)), as in Article I's households annex. Jesus' quotation presupposes the law in an argument about honouring parents and does not apply it (rule 4). These are not private killings and have no bearing on K1's label.
rows.verification: Deuteronomy 21:18 to 21: VERIFIED (search) in Article I's households annex (row CH-1, Christianity.com, KJV), not re-checked. The rest: UNVERIFIED (not searched).

rows.reference: Joshua 7:24 to 26; 2 Samuel 21:1 to 14 (Douay-Rheims 2 Kings 21); 2 Kings 10:1 to 11 and 10:30 (Douay-Rheims 4 Kings 10), with Hosea 1:4; contrast Deuteronomy 24:16 and Ezekiel 18:20
rows.says: Achan's sons and daughters are stoned and burned with him by all Israel under Joshua. David hands seven of Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites, who hang them. On Jehu's written order the leaders of Samaria kill Ahab's seventy sons, and God tells Jehu he has done well (2 Kings 10:30); later Hosea announces punishment on Jehu's house for 'the blood of Jezreel'. Against this, the law says children shall not be put to death for their parents (Deuteronomy 24:16), and Ezekiel says a son shall not bear his father's guilt.
rows.bearing: Context (rule 5): each killing is done on a ruler's order (Joshua, David, King Jehu), so it falls under exclusion (a) and does not decide K1. It grades protection by family: children and descendants die for a parent's or ancestor's wrong, which the shared scriptures forbid elsewhere. Hosea 1:4 shows tension inside the canon over Jehu's killings.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.topic: context: excluded (before birth, own death, animals, accident)
rows.says: Ananias and Sapphira fall dead when Peter confronts them with their lie; Peter does not touch them. Youths who mock Elisha are mauled by two bears after he curses them.
rows.bearing: These are not deliberate killings by a person; the text presents the deaths as God's acts. They lie outside K1 as human conduct and are recorded so that they are not mistaken for permissions. No bearing on any label.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.says: In the parable of the pounds, a nobleman who becomes king orders the enemies who did not want him to reign to be brought and killed before him.
rows.bearing: A parable, and the speaker is a king (a ruler). Under rule 4 it is an image of final judgement, not an instruction for human conduct: Implied, does not decide. The tradition reads judgement as belonging to God (Romans 12:19, row 22).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not re-checked; earlier project research also left it unverified.

rows.reference: Exodus 20:13 (Hebrew 20:13; Deuteronomy 5:17); Matthew 5:21 to 22; Matthew 19:18; Romans 13:9; 1 John 3:15
rows.original: לֹא תִּרְצָח (lo tirtsach); πᾶς ὁ μισῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ ἀνθρωποκτόνος ἐστίν (1 John 3:15)
rows.translation: ESV (as checked for Exodus 20:13 in earlier project research); World English Bible; KJV
rows.says: You shall not murder. Jesus repeats the commandment and extends it: whoever is angry with his brother is liable to judgement. Paul lists it among the commands summed up in love of neighbour. Whoever hates his brother is a murderer.
rows.bearing: Support. K1: an Explicit core prohibition in texts every branch accepts. The Hebrew ratsach, and the tradition's reading of it (row 36), mean unlawful killing, leaving courts and war aside, which matches K1's shape. K0: Explicit; anger and hatred are named as the root of murder.

rows.reference: Genesis 9:5 to 6; Leviticus 24:17 and 24:21 to 22; Numbers 35:15
rows.original: שֹׁפֵךְ דַּם הָאָדָם בָּאָדָם דָּמוֹ יִשָּׁפֵךְ כִּי בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם (Genesis 9:6); מִשְׁפַּט אֶחָד יִהְיֶה לָכֶם כַּגֵּר כָּאֶזְרָח (Leviticus 24:22)
rows.says: God will require the life of anyone who sheds human blood, because God made humankind in his image. Whoever kills any human being is to be put to death, and there is one law for the stranger and the native. The cities of refuge serve strangers and sojourners as well as Israelites.
rows.bearing: Support for K1's scope. The worth of every human life rests on the image of God, which all people share, and the law of homicide protects the foreigner equally (Explicit). This answers the question whether protection is limited to one's own community: in the homicide law it is not. The penalties themselves are court context (exclusion (a)).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.tier: 1; Augustine 2 (all branches; not counted)
rows.reference: Luke 10:25 to 37; Matthew 5:43 to 48; Augustine, On Christian Doctrine I.30.31
rows.translation: ESV and KJV; Schaff (ed.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers (Augustine)
rows.says: Asked 'Who is my neighbour?', Jesus tells of a Samaritan, a despised outsider, who cares for a wounded man, and makes him the model of a neighbour. Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, since God sends rain on the just and the unjust. Augustine concludes that every human being is to be counted as a neighbour.
rows.bearing: Support: the duty of love, which includes not killing, reaches outsiders, enemies and 'the unjust' (Clear teaching). With row 20, this answers the scope question for K1: protection is not limited to one's own community or faith.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in earlier project research (Article I), not re-checked: esv.org (Luke 10:29 to 37); biblia.com (Matthew 5:43 to 44); ccel.org (Augustine, On Christian Doctrine I.30.31).

rows.original: μὴ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκδικοῦντες (not avenging yourselves, 12:19); ἔκδικος εἰς ὀργήν (an avenger for wrath, 13:4)
rows.says: Repay no one evil for evil. Never avenge yourselves, but leave room for God's wrath, for vengeance belongs to God; if your enemy is hungry, feed him. The ruler is God's servant, who does not bear the sword in vain and carries out wrath on the wrongdoer.
rows.bearing: Support and reconciliation. K0: an Explicit ban on private revenge in texts every branch accepts. K1: the tradition reads 12:19 together with 13:4 as reserving the sword to public authority, so no private person may kill to punish (Aquinas II-II q.64 a.3, row 30; Luther, row 36). This is the New Testament reading that narrows the avenger and zealot texts (rows 1, 6 and 7). Romans 13:4 itself is court context.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in earlier project research (Article I), not re-checked: biblia.com (Romans 12:17 to 21, KJV 1900); King James Bible Online (Romans 13:4).

rows.reference: Matthew 26:51 to 52; Luke 22:36 to 38 and 22:49 to 51; John 18:10 to 11
rows.original: πάντες γὰρ οἱ λαβόντες μάχαιραν ἐν μαχαίρῃ ἀπολοῦνται (Matthew 26:52)
rows.says: At Jesus' arrest, Peter draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. Jesus tells him to put the sword away, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword, and in Luke he heals the man. Earlier, Jesus tells the disciples to buy swords and, when shown two, says 'It is enough'.
rows.bearing: A limit on K1's exception: here even defending an innocent person (Jesus) with the sword is rebuked. The tradition differs on how far this binds (pacifist readings, against the majority view that defence is lawful), and Luke 22:36 to 38 is read both ways. It is a stricter rule than K1, so it does not contradict K1. K0: supports.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.original: ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτος ἐπ᾽ αὐτὴν βαλέτω λίθον (8:7)
rows.says: Scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery and remind Jesus that the law commands stoning. He says that whoever among them is without sin should throw the first stone. They leave one by one, and he does not condemn her, telling her to sin no more.
rows.bearing: Supports K1 against killing by a crowd, though the scene is framed as a test of the law, so it is partly court context. Textual note: the passage is missing from the earliest manuscripts. The Catholic Church treats it as canonical, and Orthodox and Protestant Bibles print it, often in brackets. It is Clear teaching that the crowd should not kill her, but it does not decide on its own.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.reference: Acts 7:54 to 8:1; John 16:2; Galatians 1:13 to 14; Philippians 3:6; Acts 22:4 and 26:9 to 11; 1 Timothy 1:13
rows.says: A crowd stones Stephen, who prays that the sin not be held against them, and Saul approves. Jesus warns that whoever kills his followers will think he is serving God. Paul later says that, in zeal for his ancestors' traditions, he persecuted the church to the death and voted against those put to death. He calls himself a former blasphemer, persecutor and violent man who acted in ignorance.
rows.bearing: Reconciliation: the New Testament presents religiously zealous killing outside any court (the Phinehas pattern) as wrongdoing, in the voice of Jesus and of the former persecutor. It supports K1 at Clear teaching level: crowds, religious leaders and zealots are bound, and heretics and dissenters are protected. Stephen's death is reported, not approved (rule 4).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.reference: Genesis 34:25 to 31 with 49:5 to 7; 1 Samuel 25:21 to 34 (Douay-Rheims 1 Kings 25); 2 Samuel 3:26 to 39 with 1 Kings 2:5 to 6 and 2:31 to 33
rows.original: אָרוּר אַפָּם כִּי עָז (cursed be their anger, for it was fierce, Genesis 49:7)
rows.says: Simeon and Levi kill the men of Shechem to avenge their sister, and Jacob curses their anger and fury. Abigail stops David from avenging himself with his own hand, and David blesses her for keeping him from bloodshed. Joab kills Abner to avenge his brother; David disowns the act, and Solomon later punishes Joab for shedding 'the blood of war in peace'.
rows.bearing: Support for K0 at Clear teaching level in texts every branch accepts: killing out of anger or revenge, on one's own authority, is condemned, even when the victim had wronged one's family.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.reference: 2 Samuel 11 to 12; 1 Kings 21 (Douay-Rheims 3 Kings 21); Proverbs 1:10 to 19
rows.says: King David arranges Uriah's death in order to take his wife, and the prophet Nathan condemns him in God's name. King Ahab and Jezebel have Naboth falsely tried and stoned to take his vineyard, and Elijah announces God's judgement. Proverbs warns the young not to join those who lie in wait for blood to fill their houses with plunder.
rows.bearing: Support for K0 (killing for gain): Explicit in Proverbs and Clear teaching in the narratives. The narratives condemn even kings who kill for gain, including through a sham court (Naboth).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.reference: Exodus 1:15 to 21; Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2 to 5; Psalm 106:37 to 38 (Septuagint and Vulgate 105:37 to 38); Jeremiah 7:31; Matthew 2:16 to 18
rows.says: Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives to kill newborn boys. They refuse, and God deals well with them. The law forbids giving children to Molech, on pain of death. The same psalm that praises Phinehas condemns Israel for sacrificing sons and daughters, 'innocent blood'. Jeremiah says that burning children was something God never commanded. Herod's killing of the infants of Bethlehem is told as a grief.
rows.bearing: Support for K1 from birth onwards (rule 9). Killing newborns and children, including by parents for religious reasons, is condemned at Explicit level in texts every branch accepts. This answers the question whether the texts allow killing newborns: the shared scriptures condemn it.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.tier: 2 (all branches; not counted)
rows.original: οὐ φονεύσεις τέκνον ἐν φθορᾷ οὐδὲ γεννηθὲν ἀποκτενεῖς (Didache 2.2)
rows.says: The earliest Christian manual of conduct commands: do not murder a child by abortion, nor kill one that has been born. The Epistle to Diognetus says Christians marry and have children like everyone else, but do not expose (cast away) their offspring.
rows.bearing: Supports K1 for newborns (Explicit, Tier 2); the abortion clause is context only (exclusion (c)). It shows the tradition's early stand against infanticide and the exposure of infants, both common in the Greco-Roman world. Not counted (rule 1).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched in this run; earlier project research verified Didache 1.2 only.

rows.tier: 2 (Catholic classical authority; not counted)
rows.branch: Catholic (the quoted Augustine is honoured by all branches)
rows.reference: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, question 64, article 3 (body, sed contra and objection 1)
rows.original: ad illum solum pertinet cui committitur cura communitatis conservandae (Latin from memory)
rows.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920)
rows.says: Killing an evildoer is lawful only so far as it serves the welfare of the whole community. So it belongs only to the one entrusted with the community's care, as a physician may cut off a diseased limb; a private individual may not do it. The sed contra quotes Augustine: whoever kills an evildoer without public authority will be judged a murderer. The first objection cites Moses' order to the Levites (Exodus 32:27).
rows.bearing: Reconciliation. For Catholics it states explicitly K1's rule that no one may kill on private authority (defence is treated separately, row 33). The Augustine quotation carries the rule back to a Father that all branches honour. It narrows the Old Testament zealot and avenger texts (rows 1, 6 and 7) to public authority or a direct divine command. Not counted (rule 1).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): ccel.org; the body, the sed contra and objection 1 were seen in the results, but the reply to objection 1 was not.

rows.tier: 2 (Catholic classical authority; not counted)
rows.reference: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, question 64, article 6, with the reply to objection 1
rows.original: nullo modo licet occidere innocentem (Latin from memory)
rows.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920)
rows.says: Since the life of the righteous preserves and furthers the common good, it is in no way lawful to kill an innocent person. In reply to the objection about Abraham: God is Lord of death and life, by whose decree both sinners and the righteous die. So one who kills an innocent person at God's command does not sin, and Abraham did not sin in consenting to kill his son.
rows.bearing: Reconciliation and limit. It teaches K1 for the innocent (Explicit, Catholic Tier 2), with no exception for status. But it keeps one exception K1 does not have: a direct command of God. This is how the tradition explains Abraham (row 11) and, on some readings, Phinehas and the commanded wars (rows 1 and 39). Scholarship (Weiss 2017) reads the exception as narrow. Because the exception rests on God's own command, not on any human authority, the tradition's floor differs from K1 at one point in principle. This supports the Unclear label rather than Taught.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): ccel.org (the body and the reply to objection 1, including Abraham, were seen in the results); Weiss (2017), University of Cambridge repository, on the narrowness of the exception.

rows.tier: 2 (Church Father; all branches; not counted)
rows.translation: Marcus Dods (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 2)
rows.says: Augustine names the exceptions to 'You shall not kill'. They are those whom God commands to be killed, by a general law or by a special command for a time, and those whom soldiers or magistrates put to death by public authority. Abraham was praised for his readiness, and whether Jephthah acted at God's command is left open. Outside these cases, whoever kills a human being, himself or another, is guilty of murder. Samson's death is excused by a secret command of the Spirit.
rows.bearing: Reconciliation: the classical statement of the tradition's floor, honoured by all branches. There is no private killing; killing is allowed only by public authority or at a direct divine command. It matches K1 on private authority and adds the divine-command exception (as in row 31). Not counted (rule 1).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched in this run; content from memory, to be checked in Book I on New Advent or CCEL.

rows.tier: 2 (Augustine: all branches; Aquinas: Catholic; not counted)
rows.reference: Augustine, Letter 47.5 (to Publicola) and On Free Choice of the Will I.5; Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, question 64, article 7
rows.translation: Schaff (ed.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers (Augustine); Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Aquinas)
rows.says: Augustine does not approve of killing another to save one's own life, unless one is a soldier or public official acting for others or for the city. In On Free Choice he doubts that a private person who kills an attacker is free of fault before God, though the human law that allows it is not unjust. Aquinas allows private self-defence with moderate force, where the attacker's death is not intended but follows (the 'double effect'); only public authority may intend to kill.
rows.bearing: A limit on K1's exception. The classical authorities are stricter than K1 about private defence (Augustine), or allow it only without the intention to kill (Aquinas). A stricter rule does not contradict K1; it shows how the tradition fences the exception.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.tier: 2 (Aquinas: Catholic; Westminster: Reformed; Thirty-Nine Articles: Anglican; not counted)
rows.reference: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, question 104, article 3; Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) 19.4; Thirty-Nine Articles (1571), Article 7
rows.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920); original English texts
rows.says: Aquinas: the judicial precepts of the Old Law were annulled by the coming of Christ, though keeping them is not deadly. Westminster Confession: the judicial laws given to Israel as a body politic expired with that state and bind no further than their 'general equity' requires. Thirty-Nine Articles: the civil precepts of the law of Moses need not be received in any commonwealth.
rows.bearing: Reconciliation for the Old Testament laws of the blood avenger, the enticer, the night thief and the slave (rows 6, 7, 9 and 10): they lose their binding force for Christians without being condemned. It does not reach the narratives that praise individual acts (Phinehas, row 1). Not counted (rule 1).
rows.verification: Aquinas: VERIFIED (search) in earlier project research (ccel.org; New Advent), not re-checked. Westminster Confession 19.4 and Thirty-Nine Articles 7: UNVERIFIED.

rows.tier: outside the corpus as listed (Protestant commentator; not counted)
rows.reference: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1708 to 1710), on Numbers 25:7 to 13
rows.says: Henry praises Phinehas's 'courage of zeal and faith', but says the act 'can never be an example' for private revenge, religious persecution or irregular public vengeance.
rows.bearing: Protestant reconciliation: Phinehas is read as an extraordinary act that is not to be copied, which narrows row 1. Not counted (rule 1); it is a widely used Protestant commentary, not a confession. Another, unnamed verse-by-verse commentary in the same search results reads the act as done with public authority; the two readings together show that the judicial or private character is disputed (rule 5).

rows.tier: 2 (branch-specific; not counted); the Westminster Larger Catechism is outside the corpus as listed (only the Confession is listed)
rows.reference: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2261, 2263 to 2265 and 2268; Martin Luther, Large Catechism (1529), Fifth Commandment; Heidelberg Catechism (1563), Questions 105 to 106; Westminster Larger Catechism (1648), Questions 135 to 136
rows.translation: Official English (Catechism of the Catholic Church); standard English translations (Luther, Heidelberg); original English (Westminster)
rows.says: Catholic Catechism: the deliberate murder of an innocent person is gravely contrary to human dignity, and the law forbidding it binds everyone, always and everywhere (2261); legitimate defence is allowed, and may be a duty for those responsible for others (2263 to 2265); infanticide, parricide and the murder of a spouse are especially grave (2268). Luther: the commandment binds every individual, while God and the government, which punish evildoers, are not included. Heidelberg: do not hate, wound or kill your neighbour, and lay aside all desire for revenge; God hates the roots of murder, which are envy, hatred, anger and the desire for revenge; the magistrate bears the sword to prevent murder. Westminster Larger Catechism: all taking of life is forbidden except in public justice, lawful war or necessary defence.
rows.bearing: Reconciliation: each major Western branch states the floor in K1's shape (no killing except by public authority, in lawful war or in necessary defence), and Heidelberg names K0's motives. Not counted (rule 1). No equivalent Orthodox statement was verified (row 37).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched in this run; wording from memory, to be checked on vatican.va and ccel.org.

rows.tier: 2 (Orthodox: Father and canon law; not counted)
rows.branch: Orthodox (Basil is honoured by all branches)
rows.reference: Basil of Caesarea, Canonical Letters (Letter 188, canons 8 and 13; Letter 199, canon 33; compare Letter 217, canon 52), ratified for the Orthodox by the Council in Trullo (692), canon 2
rows.translation: Schaff (ed.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 8
rows.says: Basil distinguishes wilful from unwilling killing and sets long penances for wilful murder (canon 8). He says the fathers did not count killing in war as murder, but advises soldiers with blood on their hands to stay away from communion for three years (canon 13). He treats a woman who gives birth by the road and leaves the child to die as guilty of murder (canon 33).
rows.bearing: Reconciliation for the Orthodox branch: newborns are protected as persons (supports K1, rule 9), and even killing in war carries a penance (context for K3). Not counted (rule 1).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched; canon numbers from memory.

rows.tier: 2 (Catholic; not counted); Dignitatis Humanae is outside the corpus as listed
rows.reference: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, question 11, article 3, and question 64, article 2, reply to objection 3; Second Vatican Council, Dignitatis Humanae 2 (1965); Catechism of the Catholic Church 2267 (2018 revision)
rows.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920); official English (vatican.va)
rows.says: Aquinas holds that obstinate heretics, after warnings, may be handed to the secular court to be removed from the world by death, and that a person who sins gravely falls from human dignity and may be put to death by public authority. The Second Vatican Council teaches that every person has a right to religious freedom, free from coercion by any human power. The 2018 Catechism calls the death penalty inadmissible, because human dignity is not lost even after the most serious crimes.
rows.bearing: Context (rule 5): these texts are about punishment by courts and rulers (exclusion (a)), so they do not decide K1, though they once graded protection by faith. Later Catholic teaching reverses the premise. Not counted (rule 1).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in earlier project research (Article I), not re-checked: ccel.org (q.11 a.3); aquinas.cc (q.64 a.2 ad 3); vatican.va (Dignitatis Humanae; Holy See Press Office bulletin of 2 August 2018 for Catechism 2267).

rows.reference: Deuteronomy 20:10 to 18; 1 Samuel 15:2 to 3, 15:9 to 23 and 15:32 to 33 (Douay-Rheims 1 Kings 15); Joshua 6:17 and 6:21; Numbers 31:7 to 18
rows.original: לֹא תְחַיֶּה כָּל נְשָׁמָה (you shall save alive nothing that breathes, Deuteronomy 20:16); מֵעֹלֵל וְעַד יוֹנֵק (from child to infant at the breast, 1 Samuel 15:3)
rows.translation: KJV; World English Bible; as displayed on Bible Gateway
rows.says: For distant cities, Israel must first offer peace; if a city fights, its men are killed and its women and children are taken. For the cities of the seven Canaanite nations, nothing that breathes is to be left alive. God, through Samuel, commands Saul to destroy Amalek: men and women, children and infants. Saul is rejected for sparing King Agag and the best animals, and Samuel himself kills Agag, a prisoner. Jericho is destroyed, young and old. After the war with Midian, Moses orders the captive boys, and the women who had lain with a man, to be killed.
rows.bearing: K3: Contradicted in texts every branch accepts. God commands, and the texts approve, the deliberate killing of people who are not fighting, including infants and prisoners (rule 2 applied to K3). K1 and K0: context only (exclusion (b)); these are wars ordered by God and the community's leaders, not private acts. Deuteronomy 20:10 to 14 (offer peace first; spare the women and children of distant cities) teaches part of K3 for ordinary wars.

rows.tier: 1; Augustine 2 (all branches; not counted)
rows.reference: Psalm 137:7 to 9 (Septuagint and Vulgate Psalm 136; Douay-Rheims 136), with Augustine, Expositions on the Psalms, on Psalm 137 (136)
rows.original: אַשְׁרֵי שֶׁיֹּאחֵז וְנִפֵּץ אֶת עֹלָלַיִךְ אֶל הַסָּלַע (happy is he who seizes and dashes your little ones against the rock, 137:9)
rows.says: Exiles by the rivers of Babylon pray against Edom and Babylon: happy is he who repays Babylon as she has done to them, who dashes her little ones against the rock. Augustine reads Babylon's little ones as sinful desires at their birth, to be dashed against the rock, which is Christ.
rows.bearing: K3 and K0: a prayer of grief that calls blessed whoever kills an enemy's infants in revenge for a war. It is a lament addressed to God, not a command to anyone. Under rule 4 it is Implied for any approval of human conduct, and it is war context (exclusion (b)). The tradition's main reading is allegorical (Augustine; UNVERIFIED), and the New Testament forbids personal vengeance (Romans 12:19). It does not decide; K3 is decided by row 39.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched; earlier project research also left it unexamined.

rows.says: God condemns Ammon for ripping open pregnant women in Gilead to enlarge its border. Elisha weeps because Hazael will burn Israel's fortresses, kill its young men, dash its children and rip open its pregnant women. John the Baptist tells soldiers to extort from no one by violence or false accusation, and to be content with their wages.
rows.bearing: K3: teaches in part (Clear teaching), in texts every branch accepts, that atrocities against non-combatants in wars of conquest are wrong; Luke 3:14 limits soldiers' conduct towards civilians. These do not cancel the commanded destruction in row 39, so K3 stays Contradicted.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched.

rows.tier: 2 (Augustine: all branches; Aquinas: Catholic; not counted)
rows.reference: Augustine, Contra Faustum XXII.74 to 75; Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, question 40, article 1
rows.translation: R. Stothert (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 4); Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920)
rows.says: Augustine, answering the Manichaean Faustus, defends Moses' wars as obedience to God. What is blamed in war is the love of violence and cruelty, and a just war needs the ruler's authority or, in Israel's case, God's command. Aquinas: a private person may not declare war, since he can seek redress from his superior; war needs the ruler's authority, a just cause and a right intention.
rows.bearing: Reconciliation for K3 and context for K1. The commanded destruction is defended as a unique divine command, not disowned, and private war is excluded. Later authorities never outweigh a contradicting counted text (METHOD.md section 9, decision 7), so K3 stays Contradicted. Not counted (rule 1).

rows.tier: 2 (Catechism: Catholic; Origen: Father, all branches; not counted); Vitoria and Gaudium et Spes are outside the corpus as listed
rows.reference: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2313 to 2314 (quoting Second Vatican Council, Gaudium et Spes 80); Francisco de Vitoria, On the Law of War (1539); Origen, Homilies on Joshua
rows.says: Catechism: non-combatants, wounded soldiers and prisoners must be respected and treated humanely, and any act of war aimed at destroying whole cities with their inhabitants without distinction is a crime against God and man. counter.reconciliation:
Christianity reconciles its hard texts in five ways. Most of the authorities below are verified only in part.

(1) Only public authority may kill a wrongdoer. In the New Testament (Tier 1, all branches), Romans 12:17 to 21 forbids private vengeance, and Romans 13:1 to 4 gives the sword to the ruler as God's 'revenger' (verified in earlier project research). Augustine, a Father honoured by all branches, is quoted in the sed contra of Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II q.64 a.3: whoever kills an evildoer without public authority is a murderer (verified, ccel.org). Aquinas, a classical Catholic authority (Tier 2), restricts killing wrongdoers to those entrusted with the community's care (verified). The branch catechisms state the same shape, though none was verified here: Catholic Catechism 2261 to 2268; Luther's Large Catechism (God and the government are not included in the commandment); Heidelberg Questions 105 to 106 (envy, hatred, anger and the desire for revenge are the roots of murder); Westminster Larger Catechism Question 136 (no taking of life except in public justice, lawful war or necessary defence; outside the corpus as listed).

(2) Never the innocent, except at God's direct command. Aquinas II-II q.64 a.6 (verified) holds that it is in no way lawful to kill the innocent. In reply to the objection about Abraham, he says that one who kills at God's command does not sin, because God is Lord of life and death. Augustine, City of God I.21 (unverified), lists the same exceptions: public authority, and a general or special command of God. The tradition uses this to explain Abraham, the commanded wars and, on some readings, Phinehas and Samson, as unique divine commands that cannot be repeated, not as precedents. Scholarship (Weiss 2017, verified) reads the exception as narrow. Even so, it is an exception K1 does not contain.

(3) The judicial laws of the Old Testament no longer bind. Aquinas I-II q.104 a.3 (Catholic; verified in earlier research) says they were annulled by Christ. The Westminster Confession 19.4 (Reformed; unverified) says they expired with Israel's state, apart from their 'general equity'. The Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 7 (Anglican; unverified), say Moses' civil precepts bind no commonwealth. This covers the blood avenger (Numbers 35), the enticer (Deuteronomy 13), the night thief (Exodus 22:2 to 3) and the slave law (Exodus 21:20 to 21). It ends their force without condemning them, and it does not reach narratives that praise individual acts.

(4) Zeal is not a licence. Within Tier 1, Jesus rebukes the disciples who wanted to destroy a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54 to 55, verified in earlier research). He turns a crowd away from stoning (John 8:2 to 11, textually disputed, unverified), and he foretells that his followers' killers will think they serve God (John 16:2). Paul calls his own zealous persecution violent and done in ignorance (Galatians 1:13 to 14; 1 Timothy 1:13; unverified). Matthew Henry, a Protestant commentator outside the corpus as listed, says Phinehas's act 'can never be an example' for private revenge, religious persecution or irregular public vengeance (verified through search). Another commentary in the same results reads Phinehas as acting with public authority. The Psalm 106:30 verb ('executed judgment', 'intervened', 'made atonement', 'pacified') is itself disputed. So the tradition is divided on whether Phinehas acted privately, and no verified classical Catholic or Orthodox authority on Phinehas was found: the lead on Aquinas and 'divine instigation' could not be confirmed.

(5) On war, Augustine (Contra Faustum XXII.74 to 75, verified in earlier research) defends the herem wars as obedience to God's command rather than disowning them. Aquinas (II-II q.40 a.1, verified) denies that private persons may make war. Origen allegorises the wars of Joshua (unverified). Augustine reads Psalm 137:9 as about crushing sinful desires (unverified). Basil's canons, ratified for the Orthodox at Trullo, attach a penance even to killing in war (unverified). Modern Catholic teaching states non-combatant immunity (Catechism 2313 to 2314, citing Gaudium et Spes 80; unverified). Within Tier 1, Amos 1:13 and 2 Kings 8:12 condemn atrocities against pregnant women and children in other nations' wars (unverified).

On children, the shared scriptures condemn child sacrifice and Pharaoh's and Herod's infanticides. The Didache 2.2 (Tier 2, unverified) forbids killing a child that has been born. Basil's canon 33 (Orthodox, unverified) treats leaving a newborn to die as murder. Jephthah's sacrifice of his daughter is reported, not approved, and Jerome, quoted by Aquinas (II-II q.88 a.2 ad 2; unverified), calls the keeping of the vow wicked.

Standing: none of these reconciling authorities is a counted text. Under rule 1 and METHOD.md section 9, decision 7, they explain the tradition's reading but cannot turn a contradicting counted text into a taught one. Under rule 6, however, a narrowing by the tradition's own counted texts (here, Romans 12:19 to 13:4 and Luke 9:54 to 55) or by its classical commentators makes a hard case Unclear rather than Contradicted.

K1.label: Unclear (all branches)
K1.reason: K1's core is taught at Explicit level in texts every branch accepts. 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13, verified in earlier research) comes with a scope that reaches strangers, enemies and despised outsiders (Luke 10:29 to 37 and Matthew 5:43 to 44, verified earlier; Genesis 9:6 and Leviticus 24:22, unverified). Private vengeance is forbidden (Romans 12:17 to 21, verified earlier), religious zeal is rejected as a licence to destroy outsiders (Luke 9:54 to 55, verified earlier), and child-killing and infanticide are condemned (rows 28 and 29, unverified). But Numbers 25:6 to 13, accepted by every branch, has God approve in words Phinehas's killing of two people who were not attacking anyone, done without a trial. If that act was private, rule 2 would make the label Contradicted. The tradition disputes whether it was private: Moses had just ordered the judges to kill (25:5); Psalm 106:30's verb is rendered 'executed judgment', 'intervened', 'made atonement' or 'pacified'; and commentators read the act either as public authority or as extraordinary zeal never to be copied (Matthew Henry, verified). Rule 5 (last sentence) and rule 6 therefore give Unclear. The tradition's own reconciliation supports Unclear rather than Taught. Only public authority may kill a wrongdoer, and the innocent may never be killed except at God's direct command (Aquinas II-II q.64 a.3 and a.6, verified; Augustine, City of God I.21, unverified). That keeps a divine-command exception which K1 lacks. Further hard texts point the same way but are UNVERIFIED and do not decide yet (rule 1): the blood avenger (Numbers 35:19 to 27), the enticer (Deuteronomy 13:6 to 10, where the Septuagint reads 'report'), Psalm 106:30 to 31, and, for Catholics and Orthodox only, 1 Maccabees 2:23 to 26. What would change the label: if Phinehas is read as a private act approved by God, Contradicted (all branches, rule 2). If the partial verification of Numbers 25 (through commentary pages, not the verse page) is judged too weak, the label on verified texts alone is Taught until the hard texts are checked.

K0.label: Taught (all branches), provisional: likely Unclear once the blood-avenger law is verified
K0.reason: K0 is Explicit in verified texts every branch accepts: Romans 12:17 to 21 forbids avenging oneself (verified earlier), and Exodus 20:13 forbids murder (verified earlier). Further explicit support is unverified here: Matthew 5:21 to 22 (anger), 1 John 3:15 (hatred), Genesis 49:5 to 7, 1 Samuel 25 and 2 Samuel 3 (revenge), and Proverbs 1:10 to 19, 2 Samuel 12 and 1 Kings 21 (gain). For Reformed Protestants, Heidelberg Question 106 names envy, hatred, anger and the desire for revenge as the roots of murder (unverified). Phinehas's motive is zeal for God, not gain, anger, hatred or revenge, so the main K1 hard text bears on K0 only if zeal is read as anger (Implied). K0 therefore leaves zealot killing for religion untouched, which is exactly where Christianity's hardest texts lie. The likely hard case is the blood-avenger law (Numbers 35:19, 21 and 27; Deuteronomy 19:6 and 19:12). There a kinsman kills on a footing the law itself calls avenging, inside a procedure whose judicial or private character is disputed. Once verified, it would make the label Unclear (rules 5 and 6), not Contradicted, because the New Testament (Romans 12:19 to 13:4) and the main authorities (Aquinas I-II q.104 a.3, verified earlier) narrow it. Samson's killings for gain and revenge (Judges 14:19; 15:11; 16:28) are read as war waged by a judge under divine prompting (unverified): context, or Unclear at most.

K3.label: Contradicted (all branches)
K3.reason: In Old Testament texts accepted by every branch, God commands, and the texts approve, the deliberate killing of people who are not fighting, including infants and prisoners (rule 2 applied to K3). Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17 says to leave nothing that breathes alive (verified in earlier research). 1 Samuel 15:3 commands killing men, women, children and infants (verified in an earlier check). Numbers 31:17 has captive boys and women killed (verified in the households annex). Joshua 6:21 and Samuel's killing of the prisoner Agag (1 Samuel 15:33) are unverified. The tradition does not disown these texts. Augustine (Contra Faustum XXII.74 to 75, verified earlier) and Aquinas (II-II q.64 a.6 ad 1, verified) explain them as unique commands of God, who is Lord of life. Origen allegorises them (unverified). Tier 1 condemns atrocities against non-combatants in other wars (Amos 1:13; 2 Kings 8:12; unverified), and Deuteronomy 20:10 to 14 spares the women and children of distant cities: K3 is taught in part. Later authorities teach K3 for today: Catechism 2313 to 2314, Vitoria, and Basil's penance for killing in war (all unverified). Under METHOD.md section 9, decision 7, later authorities never outweigh a contradicting counted text. The New Testament is silent on conduct in war apart from Luke 3:14.
