rows.original: Non occides ('Thou shalt not kill', as Augustine quotes it)
rows.translation: Marcus Dods (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 2)
rows.says: The command not to kill has exceptions only by divine authority: a just general law (those who wage war at God's command or under His laws, and public officers, who are like a sword in another's hand), or a special command God gives for a time to a person (Abraham's readiness to sacrifice Isaac; Samson; whether Jephthah acted at God's command is left open). Anyone else who kills a person, himself or another, is guilty of murder.
rows.bearing: The tradition's classical reading: no private killing; exceptions for public authority and for a direct divine command. It names no private right of self-defence (stricter than K1 there), but keeps a divine-command exception that K1 lacks. Not counted (rule 1). Killing oneself (I.20) is context only (exclusion (d)).

rows.original: גֹּאֵל הַדָּם הוּא יָמִית אֶת הָרֹצֵחַ (35:19); וְרָצַח גֹּאֵל הַדָּם אֶת הָרֹצֵחַ אֵין לוֹ דָּם (35:27; the verb in 35:27 is from memory, not checked)
rows.translation: KJV ('revenger of blood'), as displayed on Christianity.com and Bible Hub; English Revised and Webster compared; WEB has 'avenger of blood'
rows.says: The 'avenger of blood', the dead person's next of kin, is himself to put a murderer to death when he meets him (35:19, 21). One who killed without intent is judged by the congregation and must stay in a city of refuge until the high priest dies. If he leaves it and the avenger kills him there, the avenger 'shall not be guilty of blood' (35:27).
rows.bearing: The strongest counted text against K1 and K0. In 35:27 a kinsman, whom rule 5 names as a private actor, is declared wholly blameless for killing a person the congregation had found to be an unintentional killer and who is no threat, because of what the victim did (leaving the refuge): on the plain words of rules 2 and 5 that is Contradicted, for all branches. It is Unclear rather than Contradicted because (1) the counted texts set the avenger inside a scheme of judgement (35:12, 24 to 25; Deuteronomy 19:12; unverified), so whether he acts as the law's executor (exclusion (a)) or privately is disputed (rule 5, last sentence); and (2) the tradition's own counted texts forbid private vengeance and give the sword to rulers (Romans 12:19 to 13:4, verified in project records), and its classical commentators confine killing of wrongdoers to public authority (Aquinas II-II q.64 a.3, quoting Augustine), which is a narrowing reading (rule 6). For K0, 'go'el' means 'redeemer' or kinsman, not literally 'avenger', and the motive is not stated in 35:27; Deuteronomy 19:6 ('while his heart is hot', unverified) points to anger. If the lead treats the New Testament prohibition as an annulment under decision 7 (as Aquinas's annulment was treated in the households annex) and reads the avenger as private, the label is Contradicted (all branches).

rows.reference: Numbers 25:1 to 13, especially 25:4 to 8 and 25:10 to 13
rows.original: בְּקַנְאוֹ אֶת קִנְאָתִי (in being zealous with my zeal, 25:11; from memory)
rows.translation: World English Bible and KJV, paraphrased; content as shown in commentary pages
rows.says: Israelite men join the worship of Baal Peor and a plague breaks out. God tells Moses to hang the chiefs, and Moses tells Israel's judges to kill the men who joined Baal Peor (25:4 to 5). An Israelite man brings a Midianite woman into his tent; Phinehas, grandson of Aaron the priest, follows with a spear and kills them both, and the plague stops. God says Phinehas turned his anger away by being zealous with His zeal, and gives him a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood.
rows.bearing: God approves in words the deliberate killing, without trial, of two people who were not attacking anyone (rule 4 is met). If Phinehas acted as a private zealot, rule 2 would make K1 Contradicted in every branch. It is disputed whether the act was private: it follows Moses' order to the judges (25:5, unverified), Phinehas was of the priestly line, Psalm 106:30 is rendered 'executed judgment' in some versions, and commentators read it either as public authority or as extraordinary zeal never to be copied (Matthew Henry). So rules 5 and 6 give Unclear. K0: the motive is zeal for God; 'qin'ah' also means jealousy or ardour, so whether it is anger is a disputed word (Implied at most). K3: not war in this passage.

rows.says: Judith prays to the God of her father Simeon, to whom God gave a sword to take vengeance on the strangers who defiled a virgin (the Shechem story). Judith's words are a prayer, but they ascribe the sword to God, which may count as approval (rule 4); Judith is deuterocanonical and cannot carry a finding alone. Jubilees is scripture only for the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. If that church is a major branch under METHOD.md section 9, decision 3, a verified Jubilees 30 could make K0 and K1 'Contradicted in one branch' (rule 3), unless the attack on Shechem is read as war (exclusion (b)).

rows.reference: Deuteronomy 13:6 to 11 (Hebrew 13:7 to 12), with 13:1 to 5, 17:2 to 7, and Exodus 22:18 and 22:20 (Hebrew 22:17 and 22:19)
rows.original: כִּי הָרֹג תַּהַרְגֶנּוּ (you shall surely kill him, Hebrew 13:10); Septuagint ἀναγγέλλων ἀναγγελεῖς περὶ αὐτοῦ (you shall surely report concerning him); both from memory
rows.translation: KJV and World English Bible (Hebrew text); L. C. L. Brenton (Septuagint)
rows.says: If a brother, son, daughter, wife or closest friend secretly urges you to serve other gods, do not pity or shield them; the Hebrew says 'you shall surely kill him; your hand shall be first upon him', then all the people stone him. The Septuagint reads 'you shall surely report concerning him' and, as recalled, keeps 'your hands shall be upon him among the first to slay him'. Deuteronomy 17:2 to 7 requires two or three witnesses and a judgement, and gives the witnesses' hands the first stroke.
rows.bearing: On the Hebrew wording alone it can read as a private killing of a family member for religious enticement. But the 'hand first' clause matches the role Deuteronomy 17:7 gives to witnesses in a court execution, and the Septuagint adds a report to the authorities, so the tradition's reading is judicial (exclusion (a)); at most Unclear (rules 5 and 6). It grades protection by faith. Christian reconciliation: rows on Aquinas I-II q.104 a.3, 1 Corinthians 5:13 and Luke 9:54 to 55.

rows.original: וְהִרְגוּ אִישׁ אֶת אָחִיו (and kill every man his brother, 32:27; from memory)
rows.says: After the golden calf, Moses says 'Thus says the LORD' and tells the Levites to go through the camp and kill brother, friend and neighbour. About three thousand die, and Moses tells them they have consecrated themselves, every man against his son and his brother.
rows.bearing: The order comes from Moses as leader and judge of the people, in God's name: exclusion (a). The victims include sons and brothers, so household members. If Moses is treated as a religious leader acting on his own authority rather than as a ruler, it becomes a hard case for K1 (Unclear, rule 6). Aquinas raises it as objection 1 to his rule that only public authority may kill; his reply (from memory) is that those who kill at God's command act by God's authority, like a sword in the hand.

rows.says: God tells Abraham to offer his son Isaac. Abraham binds him and takes the knife, but an angel stops him. The New Testament praises Abraham's faith.

What is praised is readiness and faith, and no killing occurs, so it is Implied (rule 4) and does not decide. Augustine (City of God I.21) and Aquinas (II-II q.64 a.6 ad 1) treat it as a special divine command, not a general permission.

Reconciliation: Jerome, quoted by Aquinas (II-II q.88 a.2 ad 2), calls the vow foolish and its keeping wicked (UNVERIFIED); Augustine (City of God I.21, verified) leaves open whether he acted at God's command.

verified.reconciliation:
Christianity reconciles its hard texts on killing in five ways. None of the authorities below is a counted text except where a Tier 1 passage is named.

(1) Only public authority may kill a wrongdoer, and private vengeance is forbidden. In Tier 1, Romans 12:17 to 21 forbids avenging oneself, and Romans 13:4 gives the sword to the ruler (both verified in project records). Classical voices make the same point. Aquinas (II-II q.64 a.3, verified by the counter researcher) quotes Augustine: whoever kills an evildoer without public authority is a murderer. Augustine (City of God I.21, verified by the support researcher) allows killing only under a just general law or a special command of God. The branch catechisms state the same structure: Catholic Catechism 2261 to 2268, Luther's Large Catechism, Heidelberg Q.105 to 106, and the Westminster Larger Catechism Q.136 (all unverified; the last is outside the corpus as listed).

(2) The innocent may never be killed, except at God's direct command. Aquinas II-II q.64 a.6 with ad 1 (verified by the counter researcher) and Augustine I.21 use this to explain Abraham, the commanded wars and, on some readings, Phinehas and Samson as unrepeatable divine commands. This is an exception K1 does not contain. It is Tier 2 and decides nothing (rule 1).

(3) The judicial laws of the Old Testament no longer bind. Aquinas I-II q.104 a.3 (verified in project records), the Westminster Confession 19.4 and the Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 7 (both unverified) say this. It covers the blood avenger, the enticer, the night thief and the slave laws. Under decision 7 and the households annex precedent it ends their force without condemning them, so on its own it removes no contradiction.

(4) Counted New Testament texts narrow the Old Testament permissions. Romans 12:19 forbids private vengeance. Matthew 5:38 to 39 sets aside retaliation, and Matthew 19:8 treats a Mosaic permission as a concession (both unverified). Luke 9:54 to 55 rebukes zeal that would destroy outsiders (verified in project records). 1 Corinthians 5:13 turns Deuteronomy's execution formula into excommunication (unverified). Within the Old Testament itself, the cities of refuge, the congregation's judgement and the elders' role (Numbers 35:12, 24 to 25; Deuteronomy 19; Joshua 20), the king's restraint of the avenger (2 Samuel 14) and God's protection of Cain (Genesis 4:15) set the avenger inside a scheme of judgement (all unverified). This narrowing by counted texts and classical commentators is what rule 6 recognises, and it is the basis for Unclear rather than Contradicted on Numbers 35:27 and Numbers 25.

(5) On war, Augustine (Contra Faustum XXII.74 to 75, verified in project records) defends the commanded wars as obedience to God rather than disowning them. Aquinas (II-II q.40 a.1) denies that private persons may make war. Origen allegorises Joshua's wars, Basil attaches a penance even to killing in war, and the Catholic Catechism (2313 to 2314) teaches immunity for non-combatants (all unverified). These later authorities do not outweigh Deuteronomy 20:16 or Numbers 31:17 (decision 7).

On children, the shared scriptures condemn child sacrifice and Pharaoh's and Herod's infanticides (Exodus 1 verified; the rest unverified). The Didache, Diognetus, Basil and the Ante-Nicene apologists condemn killing or exposing newborns (Tier 2, unverified). On slaves, Exodus 21:20 punishes killing a slave (verified), while 21:21 leaves a master unpunished when the beaten slave lingers. The tradition's reading of intent there was not checked.

K1.reason: Taught at Explicit level in counted texts every branch accepts: Exodus 20:13; Genesis 9:5 to 6, which reaches every human being as made in God's image; Matthew 5:21 to 22; and Romans 13:9 to 10 as a wider no-harm rule, whose 'neighbour' reaches everyone through Luke 10:29 to 37 (Clear teaching). Named groups are protected: newborns (Exodus 1:15 to 21, rule 9), slaves (Exodus 21:20), foreigners (2 Samuel 12:9; Jeremiah 22:3) and religious outsiders (Luke 9:54 to 55). Against this stands Numbers 35:26 to 27, verified for 35:27 by the support researcher only. A kinsman who kills a person the congregation found to be an unintentional killer, because he left the city of refuge, 'shall not be guilty of blood'. On the plain words of rules 2 and 5, which name a kinsman as a private actor, that is a contradiction. Rule 6 makes it Unclear: the counted texts place the avenger inside a scheme of judgement (Numbers 35:12, 24 to 25; Deuteronomy 19:12; unverified), so whether he acts judicially or privately is disputed (rule 5, last sentence). The tradition's own counted texts (Romans 12:19 to 13:4, verified in project records) and classical commentators (Aquinas II-II q.64 a.3 quoting Augustine, verified by the counter researcher) also narrow private killing to public authority. Numbers 25:6 to 13 (Phinehas; God approves; private or judicial disputed; verified only through commentary pages) is a second hard case of the same kind. Exodus 21:21 is Unclear (intent disputed; verified in project records). Exodus 22:2 to 3, Deuteronomy 13 and 1 Kings 18:40 are unverified or Implied, and Genesis 22 and Judges 11 are Implied (rule 4). The divine-command exception in Aquinas and Augustine is Tier 2 and decides nothing. The label depends on a disputed reading. It becomes Contradicted (all branches) if the lead treats the New Testament prohibition of private vengeance as an annulment under decision 7 (as Aquinas's annulment was treated in the households annex) and reads the avenger in 35:27 as acting on his own authority. It becomes Taught only if the avenger is read as the law's executor (exclusion (a)) and Phinehas as judicial. K0.label: Unclear (all branches)

Revenge: Romans 12:17 to 21 (verified in project records), with Leviticus 19:18 (taught in part). Gain: Deuteronomy 27:25 and 2 Samuel 12:9. Anger and envy: Matthew 5:21 to 22 and Genesis 4. Hatred: 1 John 3:15 (fellow believers), widened by Luke 6:27 to 35 and Matthew 5:43 to 48 (verified in project records). The counter researcher's 'Taught, provisional' assumed the avenger law was unverified, but Numbers 35:27 is verified by the support researcher. That text is decisive here. A kinsman known in the text as the 'avenger of blood' kills an unintentional slayer outside the refuge and is declared guiltless. Deuteronomy 19:6 ('while his heart is hot', unverified) points to anger. As for K1, whether this is judicial or private is disputed, and Romans 12:19 narrows it, so rules 5 and 6 give Unclear. Two disputed words add to this: 'go'el' means kinsman or redeemer, not literally avenger; and 'zeal' in Numbers 25:11 may or may not be anger. Samson (Judges 14 to 16), 1 Maccabees 2:24 (Catholic and Orthodox) and Psalm 137:9 are unverified, Implied or war context. If the Numbers 35:27 verification is not accepted because the verifier could not re-check it, the label on rows found in project records alone would be Taught (all branches), provisional. If the avenger is read as private and the New Testament narrowing as an annulment, it is Contradicted (all branches). Separately, an unverified Jubilees 30 could make K0 Contradicted in the Ethiopian Orthodox branch, if that is a major branch.

K3.label: Contradicted (all branches)
K3.reason: Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17 (Tier 1, every branch; verified in the Article I research record with its own Bible Gateway link) commands that nothing that breathes be left alive in the cities of the seven nations. Numbers 31:17 (verified in households annex row JU-17, link to 31:18) has the lawgiver order the killing of captured boys and of women. These are deliberate killings of people who are not fighting, commanded or approved within the text (rules 2 and 4). 1 Samuel 15:3 (infants and nursing babies), Joshua 6:21 and 1 Samuel 15:33 are UNVERIFIED and not needed. Tier 1 teaches K3 in part: Deuteronomy 20:10 to 14, 2 Kings 6:21 to 23, Amos 1:13 and Luke 3:14 (all unverified). The tradition explains the commands as unique divine commissions (Augustine, Contra Faustum XXII.74 to 75; Aquinas II-II q.64 a.6 ad 1). It teaches non-combatant immunity today (Catechism 2313 to 2314; Vitoria; Basil's penance for killing in war; all unverified). Later authorities never outweigh a contradicting counted text (decision 7). K3 is a record wording and does not affect the floor.

verified.fairness_notes:
1. The deciding texts for K1 and K0 (Numbers 35:27; Numbers 25) and for K3 (Deuteronomy 20:16; Numbers 31:17) are shared with Judaism. They must be weighed the same way in both files. The only legitimate difference is each tradition's own counted reconciliation: the Talmud (Makkot; Sanhedrin 81b to 82a) for Rabbinic Judaism, and the New Testament (Romans 12:19 to 13:4; Matthew 5:38 to 39) for Christianity. If Judaism gets Unclear on the avenger because the Talmud narrows it, Christianity should get the same label because Romans 12:19 narrows it, and the reverse also holds.
2. Consistency with the households annex. There, Exodus 21:20 to 21 made Christianity Contradicted for the no-cruelty wording, despite New Testament no-harm texts. Here I treat Romans 12:19 as a narrowing that gives Unclear. The distinction I rely on is that Romans 12:19 forbids the very act type (private vengeance), whereas no New Testament text addressed a master's beating directly. The lead should confirm this distinction. If it is rejected, Numbers 35:27 should make K1 and K0 Contradicted for both Christianity and Judaism (absent a counted narrowing), and the same test should be applied to any other tradition whose counted texts permit a kinsman's revenge.
3. Who counts as a 'ruler'. Moses (Exodus 32; Numbers 31), Samuel, Elijah and Phinehas are prophets or priests who also lead the community. Whether they are 'rulers' (exclusion (a)) or 'religious leaders' bound by K1 changes results. The same choice must be made for prophet-leaders in other traditions, for example the Prophet as ruler in Medina, or the Sikh Gurus.
4. The divine-command exception in Augustine and Aquinas is Tier 2 and explains past texts only. If it is ever counted against Christianity, any tradition with a similar doctrine must be treated the same way.
5. Many rows are UNVERIFIED only because the shared search budget ran out before the verifier could search. Matthew 19:18, Psalm 106:37 to 38, Matthew 26:52 and Exodus 22:2 to 3 are well known. An adherent should not read 'UNVERIFIED' as doubt about the texts. The labels do not depend on any of them.
6. K3 Contradicted rests on ancient commands that every Christian branch reads as unique and unrepeatable, and that later Christian teaching opposes for today. Other traditions with commanded-destruction texts should be labelled by the same rule.
7. Translation. 'Kill' (KJV) and 'murder' (modern versions) for ratsach, 'revenger' or 'avenger' for go'el, and 'executed judgment', 'intervened' or 'made atonement' for pillel (Psalm 106:30) all bear on the labels. They should be stated in sources/translations.md so that the readings are visible.
